newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar left alone in UK match-rigging trial.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar left alone in UK match-rigging trial.

text.p: Zimbabwe-born goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar will be left in the dock alone on Friday after his three co-defendants in Britain's soccer match-rigging trial walked free.

Grobbelaar was cleared on Thursday of one charge of attempting to fix matches in England's Premier soccer league, but the jury said it was still undecided over a second charge that he accepted 2,000 pounds ($3,200) to influence the outcome of games.
Two other soccer stars, former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Dutch-born goalkeeper Hans Segers were cleared in unanimous verdicts in Britain's most sensational soccer trial.
Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim was also found unanimously not guilty, leaving Grobbelaar the lone remaining defendant.
The jury in the nine-week old trial will begin its sixth day of deliberations on Friday.
Grobbelaar, 39, who has played for his national side as well as Liverpool and Southampton, looked grim-faced as he left the court hand-in-hand with his wife.
He said only that he would be back in court the next day.
The freed defendants meanwhile emerged smiling broadly to greet the waiting media crowd.

"Its been a nightmare for 2-1/2 years, but we got the verdict we deserved," said Segers, the 35-year-old former Wimbledon goalkeeper. "Today is just an unbelievable day and it has been very emotional."
The Dutch-born player said he was ready to resume his career.
Fashanu, 33, who declined to testify during the court proceedings, said he was not bitter at having had to face two trials.
"Now all I want to do is get on with my beautiful wife and go back to my friends," he said.
The former Aston Villa and Wimbledon striker is now a popular television presenter and a highly successful businessman.
The four had all denied the allegations that they were involved with an Asian gambling syndicate.

The prosecution had investigated huge cash sums the defendants deposited in their bank accounts and traced dozens of telephone calls they made to one another, but the jury concluded that these were not evidence that they had been rigging matches.
It was the second time the four had faced trial in the case. Another jury was dismissed earlier this year after failing to reach verdicts.
The case is reported to have cost millions of pounds and has shaken the image of British football.
The English Football Association announced after Thursday's verdicts that it was carrying out a detailed inquiry into the rules on betting and forecasting in the game.
The former Deputy Commissioner of London's Metropolitan Police, Sir John Smith, who is leading the inquiry is due to report back within three months.
